assumptions: THE ARCHIVED DDL AT `20260804130000_event_provider_foundation.sql:67-88` IS THE COLUMN CONTRACT, AND IT IS COMPLETE. It was cross-checked column by column against the selects and writes of all five consumers and every column they name is present. Two checks the inbound handoff did not make are made here: (a) `bandsintown/connect/route.ts:49` writes `connection_mode: mode` where `mode` is `getBandsintownMode()` and the exported type is `"disabled" | "artist_owned_key" | "partner"` (`lib/events/providers/flags.ts:43`) - the route early-returns 503 when mode is `disabled`, so only the two CHECK-allowed values can reach the column and the archived CHECK is complete rather than merely convenient; (b) NO consumer writes `secret_reference` at all, and the route that creates a connection writes none of the fields the other four read, so nothing in the reachable codebase can put a raw provider key in this table. NOTHING WAS INVENTED TO MAKE A QUERY RESOLVE, which is the failure mode this lane exists to stop.

`create table if not exists` IS NECESSARY AND ITS BLIND SPOT IS PAID FOR IN THE POST-CONDITION, NOT IGNORED. A bare `create table` is what `20260927130200_music_tracks_certification_view.sql` deliberately does for a view, and it can because for a VIEW a loud abort is the correct failure direction. A loud abort is not an option here: re-runnability is an acceptance criterion. So the guard stays, and the thing it hides is that a PRE-EXISTING relation is left completely alone - `create table if not exists` would then install RLS and grants on a table of unknown shape and report success. Out-of-band Management API application is documented by DB-002, so a pre-existing relation is a real possibility and not a hypothetical. The post-condition therefore asserts all 17 columns by NAME, TYPE, NULLABILITY and DEFAULT, every CHECK by its admitted literal set, the UNIQUE, the primary key, the foreign key WITH ITS DELETE ACTION, the index definition and the grant set - a count would not catch a re-typed column, and the premise of this file is that no column is invented.

THE GRANT TO `authenticated` IS DELIBERATELY NARROWER THAN THE ARCHIVE'S, AND THIS IS THE ONE PLACE THE FILE DOES NOT FOLLOW THE ARCHIVED DDL LITERALLY. The archive grants `select, insert, update ... to authenticated` (`20260804130000:216`); this file grants SELECT only. Two reasons, both measured. (1) All four non-status consumers resolve `.from()` through `createServiceRoleClient()`, so none needs a caller-side write grant - the five consumers need `authenticated` for exactly one SELECT. (2) The three owner-scoped policies constrain `created_by`, NOT `owner_id`, and the archive's own comment (`:188-190`) records that the owning-account check is application-side; `owner_id` is not a foreign key to any account table. So an `authenticated` INSERT would be an escalation primitive - create a connection row naming ANY `owner_id` - whose only protection would be code this table does not constrain. This is a NARROWING relative to a grant that was never issued anywhere (`local_only_unapplied`), so no live surface loses access, and a caller-side write is an additive grant in a later migration, by which time the own-row policies are already in place. The divergence is recorded here, in the migration header, and as an open question for the integrations lane; it is not a silent tightening.

THE THREE OWNER-SCOPED POLICIES ARE KEPT EVEN THOUGH THE `authenticated` GRANT MAKES INSERT AND UPDATE UNREACHABLE. They are not decoration and not legacy: they are the guard that is already correct if a later migration adds a write grant, and the post-condition asserts all three exist with their exact predicates, so their presence is a checked fact rather than an assumption. The alternative - deleting them because the grant makes them dead - would remove the only thing standing between a future write grant and an owner_id escalation.

A `to service_role` POLICY IS INCLUDED, AND IT IS A RESCUE RATHER THAN A CONVENIENCE. `service_role` carries BYPASSRLS on Supabase, which DB-013 and DB-014 both recorded makes `to service_role using (true)` policies unreachable noise. It is included anyway for a specific, measured reason: `bandsintown/disconnect` is REACHABLE today, so on a target where `service_role` lacks BYPASSRLS the absence of any service-role policy would make that route fail closed with 42501 and the outage this file closes would simply recur with a different status code. The alternative - omitting it - trades a possible silent functional hole on the one route this task exists to fix for tidiness. It grants `anon` and `authenticated` nothing, and it is measured in both configurations: with BYPASSRLS and with BYPASSRLS removed, read and update both succeed through the policy alone.

`secret_reference` IS A POINTER AND IS NOT GIVEN A CHECK CONSTRAINT. The archive says so in its own comment (`:66`) and INTG-007 makes the secret boundary encrypted-only and fail-closed. A check asserting 'this is not a key' cannot be written without a secret-store contract this lane does not own, and guessing one would be invention. The structural protection is the GRANT: `authenticated` holds SELECT and no write privilege, so no caller-side code path can write this column at all. Recorded as a named residual rather than solved.

THE `private`-SCHEMA STRANDED-RELATION CASE IS A REPAIR, NOT A REFUSAL, AND THAT IS THE FINDING. The harness's first revision asserted that a relation moved to `private` would make the migration refuse; it does not. `create table if not exists public.event_provider_connections` finds nothing in `public`, creates a correct and EMPTY relation, the post-condition is satisfied, and any pre-existing rows stay stranded in the other schema. Measured: 2 rows left in `private`, 0 in the freshly created `public` relation. The guard repairs the public surface and silently orphans the data, so 'the relation exists in `public`' is a Layer 0 STOP CONDITION in the preflight rather than something this file can detect. This is the same class as `20260821025543:9`, where `search_path = private, public` put `ticketing_migration_issues` where no public reader could see it.

NO `DELETE` PATH EXISTS, AND THAT IS A CHOICE. No consumer deletes a connection; `bandsintown/disconnect` sets `status = 'disconnected'` and the route's own comment records that source records are disabled rather than deleted, and preserved. So there is no DELETE policy (denied to every non-privileged caller) and no DELETE grant to `service_role`. The post-condition asserts both absences, so a future permissive delete cannot appear unnoticed. `created_by ... on delete cascade` still removes a deleted USER's connections, which is the archived contract; the consequence recorded rather than softened is that this cascade does NOT clean up the `secret_reference` pointer in the secret store, because a pointer into an external store is not a foreign key.

NO FUNCTION, TRIGGER, VIEW OR MATERIALIZED VIEW IS CREATED, so nothing is added to the routine inventory and the CP-016 regeneration delta is the single new relation. In particular the post-condition's expression normalization is four sequential `regexp_replace` calls in one loop rather than a `create function` helper: a function declared inside a plpgsql `declare` block is not valid plpgsql (a function is not a declaration), and a top-level one would add a chain routine that no consumer wants and that the regeneration delta would then have to account for.

THE POST-CONDITION NORMALIZES RENDERED EXPRESSIONS, BECAUSE A TEXTUAL COMPARISON REPORTS A HEALTHY TARGET AS A VIOLATION. `pg_get_expr` renders `public.x` as `x` when `public` is in `search_path`, and renders an inlined SQL function as `( SELECT auth.uid() AS uid)` on a target whose `auth.uid()` is a SQL function and as `auth.uid()` on a real Supabase target whose `auth.uid()` is plpgsql - and this file controls neither. That is DB-013's recorded false-failure, reintroduced in a new form. Normalization is case, `public.` qualification, an inlined-function alias, whitespace, and redundant outer parentheses applied repeatedly. ITS LIMIT IS STATED: removing balanced parentheses is not injective, so the contract entries are written to be unambiguous under it, which for four simple predicates, one index definition and seventeen column descriptors they are. The `polcmd` question is answered by the contract rather than by a branch - `using=` and `check=` are emitted for every policy and the expected list declares which is `-` - so a `FOR SELECT` policy's absent `WITH CHECK` and a `FOR INSERT` policy's absent `USING` are declared absences. That closes DB-013's defect (a) and DB-014's reintroduction of it structurally rather than by remembering not to trip over it.

`event_sync_jobs` IS A REAL CO-DEPENDENCY AND IS NOT RESTORED HERE. `bandsintown/connect/route.ts:63` upserts it and `cron/events/sync` claims it; it comes from the SAME archived file (`:95-113`) and is equally absent from the active chain. It is out of DB-020's working set and out of the integrations cluster, so it is routed rather than absorbed. Consequence stated plainly: after this file, `connect` remains 503 for a reason that is now TWO missing relations instead of one. No route becomes reachable through a half-restored pair, and the shipped surface is `status` + `disconnect`, which is what is live today.

NO TYPE REGENERATION IS NEEDED FOR THE FILE TO BE SAFE BUT IT IS NEEDED FOR THE DIAGNOSTICS TO CLEAR, AND IT IS BLOCKED. `lib/database.types.ts` is byte-unchanged (SHA-256 168daaff01fb7ef285fb7bc69cfb5876cb092491953cdbbb2cea3fa7cb7558ab7) and is NOT regenerated and NOT hand-edited. The file adds one relation, so the chain becomes one relation AHEAD of the contract: regeneration may only ADD coverage and delete nothing, which is the CP-016 superset property this file preserves. Regeneration itself remains blocked on RELEASE-013 provisioning a chain-built target, and `--linked` must never be used as a source (CP-127). The 6 diagnostics in the integrations cluster are therefore NOT claimed as cleared by this file; only an applied migration plus a real regeneration clears them, and neither happened.

THE HARNESS LIVES INSIDE THIS MANIFEST'S DIRECTORY, NOT IN `supabase/tests/`, AND THAT IS A GRANT BOUNDARY RATHER THAN A CHOICE. `supabase/tests/**` is outside DB-020's working set; `docs/engineering/migration-validation/**` is inside it. The consequence is real and is not hidden: `npm run check:db008-harness` does not run this harness, so the proof is reproducible by hand (`bash docs/engineering/migration-validation/db020_event_provider_connections.harness.sh`) and by nobody's behalf until the wiring is granted. `package.json` and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` are other lanes' files in any case.
layeredPlan: Layer 0 (preflight, read-only, operator). Run the rowCountQueries and record the result. FOUR items are STOP CONDITIONS, not warnings. (a) `public.event_provider_connections` must NOT already exist. It is expected absent on every environment; a non-NULL result means it exists out of band, and then `create table if not exists` will not touch it, this file will install RLS and grants on an unknown shape, and - if it is in a different schema - the stranded-row case measured in the harness applies: the public surface is repaired and the data is orphaned. (b) `anon`, `authenticated` and `service_role` must all exist. The revoke and the two grants are unguarded, so a target missing a role fails with 42704 - a loud, legible failure, which is why no guard wraps them. (c) `auth.users` must exist, for `created_by`'s foreign key. (d) `gen_random_uuid()` must be callable, which needs PostgreSQL 13+ built-in or `pgcrypto`; every Supabase target qualifies. Also record, without stopping on it: whether `anon` currently holds any privilege on the relation (expected no), and whether `service_role` currently holds DELETE through a platform default-privilege grant, which this file does not issue and does not revoke - see the residual in `recovery`.

Layer 1 (apply, single run, operator). One transaction, this file only, manual and explicit. Never `supabase db reset`, never `db push --include-all`, never a forced or full-chain replay (CP-051). The order inside the file is: CREATE TABLE, CREATE INDEX, COMMENT, ENABLE and FORCE RLS, four drop+create policy pairs, three grants, then the post-condition DO block. The post-condition is INSIDE the same transaction, so a target that cannot reach the asserted state fails the apply rather than reporting success. Safe to apply BEFORE any consumer change and in any order relative to every other migration: it creates one new relation, reads no existing row, writes no data row, and touches no existing object.

Layer 2 (postflight, read-only, operator). Run the postflight queries. The two that matter are the OWN-ROW probe and the ANON probe, and they must be run as at least two distinct signed-in identities plus anon, because a single-identity probe cannot distinguish own-rows-only from see-everything: user A reads 1 own connection and 0 of user B's, user B reads 0 of user A's and 1 of their own, anon's SELECT is a permission error rather than an empty list. Then run the two route-shaped selects verbatim, because they are the queries that return 500 today.

Layer 3 (no fourth layer in this lane). Three items are routed rather than absorbed: `event_sync_jobs` (same archived file, still absent, and `connect` is still 503 without it), the `authenticated` INSERT/UPDATE grant decision (recorded above; integrations owns whether a caller-side write is ever wanted), and CP-016 regeneration. None is required for this file to be safe.

SELECT rolbypassrls AS service_role_bypassrls FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname='service_role' -- expected TRUE on Supabase. FALSE is not a stop: the service_role policy in this file carries the four service-role consumers either way, and the harness measured that.

preflight.expectedAffectedRows: One relation is CREATED, empty: `public.event_provider_connections` with 17 columns, 1 primary key, 1 UNIQUE, 1 foreign key, 3 CHECK constraints and 1 partial index. RLS is enabled AND forced. Four policies are created (three own-row, one service-role). Three grants are issued: `revoke all` from `anon`, `select` to `authenticated`, `select, insert, update` to `service_role`. Three comments are attached. NO existing table, column, index, constraint, trigger, policy, grant or ROW is created, altered, dropped or narrowed, and NO data row is read for update or deleted. This migration creates the relation and writes no row to it, because no consumer can yet reach it: the two live routes only read and update a row that does not exist, and the three 503 routes cannot run.

execution.resumeStrategy: Authored - manual apply pending (CP-051). One transaction, one file. The relation is created EMPTY by this migration, so there is no data lock: CREATE TABLE takes catalog locks only, the CREATE INDEX builds over zero rows, ENABLE/FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY and GRANT take catalog locks, and the post-condition reads only catalog tables (`pg_class`, `pg_attribute`, `pg_attrdef`, `pg_constraint`, `pg_index`, `pg_policy`, `pg_roles`) and `has_table_privilege`. The lock budget is therefore independent of any existing data volume, which is a property of creating a table rather than of the statements. Safe to apply in any order relative to every other migration: this file touches no existing relation. Safe to apply BEFORE any consumer change. The file is re-runnable, so a re-apply is a no-op rather than an error.
execution.idempotency: Deterministic and repeatable, verified by applying the file FOUR times consecutively on a throwaway PostgreSQL 16.15 cluster, each in a single transaction (`psql -1`): the first three applies were consecutive and the fourth after data had been seeded. Every apply exited 0. `create table if not exists` skips on applies 2-4, the four `drop policy if exists` + `create policy` pairs re-issue cleanly, the grants are re-issued, and the post-condition passed after each. The seeded data survived: 2 rows before the fourth apply and 2 rows after, with `external_identity` intact, and exactly ONE `idx_event_provider_connections_due` after four applies. This is the property the archived `20260804130000` file's own create would also have on an empty target, but it is measured here rather than assumed, and the fourth apply is the one that matters because it is the one that ran against a populated table.

quarantine.table: public.event_provider_connections (created here; nothing is migrated into it and no existing table is read)
quarantine.strategy: No data movement, no backfill, no batch, no quarantine table. This file creates one empty relation and writes no row to it. There is no partial-application state to quarantine: the file is one transaction and its own post-condition RAISEs if the asserted state is unreachable, so a relation that ended up with the wrong column contract, the wrong policies or the wrong grants cannot be committed. The one state worth naming is the stranded-relation case measured in the harness: if a relation of this name already exists in ANOTHER schema, this file creates a correct and empty `public` one, leaves the other schema's rows where they are, and reports success. That is a Layer 0 stop condition, not a runtime branch, because detecting it and refusing would trade a loud, actionable operator message for a silent data orphan.
quarantine.lockBudget: No statement reads a row of any table. The post-condition is entirely catalog reads plus `has_table_privilege`, so it cannot queue behind a data lock, and the lock cost does not scale with the size of any catalogue. There is no statement here that holds a lock while waiting on another, so there is no deadlock ordering to get wrong.

constraints: THE THREE CHECK CONSTRAINTS ARE THE ARCHIVED ONES, AND EACH IS ASSERTED BY ITS ADMITTED LITERAL SET RATHER THAN BY NAME OR BY TEXT. `status in ('pending','active','error','disconnected')` is the set the reachable `bandsintown/disconnect` depends on - it writes `disconnected` - and `connection_mode in ('artist_owned_key','partner')` is the set `getBandsintownMode()` can produce once its `disabled` value has early-returned 503. The post-condition extracts the literal set from the rendered expression, because PostgreSQL renders an IN-list with casts that differ between versions while the admitted values do not. The harness weakens the `status` CHECK so `disconnected` is no longer storable and confirms the post-condition refuses.

THE UNIQUE (owner_type, owner_id, provider, external_identity) IS ASSERTED AS A COLUMN SET, because it is a live contract and not a detail: `bandsintown/connect/route.ts:52` upserts with exactly `onConflict: "owner_type,owner_id,provider,external_identity"`, so a UNIQUE that silently changed would turn a re-connect into a duplicate row rather than an update. The harness drops it and confirms the post-condition refuses, and separately confirms behaviourally that a duplicate on the full key is rejected while the same `external_identity` under a DIFFERENT owner is accepted - which is what a four-column key means, and which the harness's first revision asserted backwards.

THE FOREIGN KEY `created_by -> auth.users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE` IS ASSERTED WITH ITS DELETE ACTION, not merely its existence, because the cascade is what removes a deleted user's connections and a silently changed delete action is a data-retention change rather than a detail. Recorded consequence: that cascade does not clean up the `secret_reference` pointer, because a pointer into an external secret store is not a foreign key and nothing in this schema can be.

NO POLICY IS WEAKENED. There is no pre-existing policy on this relation on any environment, because the relation exists on no environment. The three own-row policies are transcribed from the archive at `:188-208` with their predicates unchanged, and the post-condition asserts each rendered predicate, so a redefinition that widened one is reported by name. An EXTRA policy - a permissive `USING (true)` SELECT is the CP-104 shape, and a DELETE policy is a delete path no consumer has - is an unexpected contract key, so the same comparison reports it in either direction.
indexes: ONE index is created: `idx_event_provider_connections_due on public.event_provider_connections (provider, next_sync_at) where status = 'active'`, transcribed from the archive at `:90-92`. The partial predicate is the point: an index for due sync work over rows that can never sync is an index that answers a question nobody asks.

The index is asserted by its WHOLE rendered `pg_get_indexdef`, including the predicate, and the harness de-icates it and confirms the post-condition refuses. That is the control for the real cost of `create index if not exists`: a same-named FULL index is kept by the guard, so only the post-condition can tell the two apart. `drop index if exists` followed by a create would be destructive, is forbidden here, and would destroy any dependent object, so the guard is kept and the definition is verified instead.

The primary key's and the UNIQUE's backing indexes are excluded from that comparison. Their column sets are already asserted by the `constraint:p:` and `constraint:u:` entries, and the primary key's backing index carries a PostgreSQL-generated name that is a naming decision rather than a decision this file makes.
constraintsAndIndexes.validationPlan: The file's own post-condition DO block is the target-side validation, and it is proven able to FAIL in NINE ways, each measured by executing the file against a deliberately broken state on a throwaway PostgreSQL 16.15: an extra permissive `USING (true)` SELECT policy; a DELETE policy; `authenticated` granted INSERT; `service_role` granted DELETE; the due index de-precated to a full index; `secret_reference` re-typed to `bytea`; `owner_id` made nullable; the `status` CHECK weakened so `disconnected` is no longer storable; and the connect `onConflict` UNIQUE dropped. Every one of the nine was reported by name, in the direction that names the defect, and every one restored its own fixture afterwards - asserted, because the first revision of this stage had a control with NO restore step and the five controls after it were therefore measured against a contaminated fixture. THREE further controls are REPAIRS rather than refusals, and the distinction is the finding rather than a naming preference: the file re-issues `alter table ... force row level security`, `revoke all ... from anon` and the grants, so out-of-band drift in those is corrected by the apply and the post-condition is never reached with the defect present. Each repair control injects the drift, asserts the catalog really moved off the wanted value, applies, and asserts the value is restored. A tenth control - a relation stranded in `private` - was RECLASSIFIED from a refusal to a repair after measurement, because the file does not refuse it: it creates a correct empty `public` relation and orphans the rows. That is recorded in `assumptions` and as a Layer 0 stop condition. Behaviourally, as real identities on the same cluster: anon is a permission error; `authenticated` INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE are all permission errors; user A reads 1 own row and 0 of user B's while user B reads 1 of their own; `service_role` holds no DELETE; and with `alter role service_role nobypassrls` applied and confirmed in the catalog, the read and the update still succeed through the service-role policy alone. A COMMITTED CONTRACT-TEST `.sql` FILE IS NOT PROVIDED, and that is a grant boundary rather than an omission: `supabase/tests/**` is outside DB-020's working set. The behavioural proof is `docs/engineering/migration-validation/db020_event_provider_connections.harness.sh` in this directory, 53 PASS / 0 FAIL, byte-identical across two runs, and it is the file whose SHA-256 is recorded above as `contractTestSha256`.

recovery.rollback: There is no data to roll back, because the relation is created empty and this file writes no row to it. Rolling back means `DROP TABLE public.event_provider_connections;` issued as a LATER FORWARD MIGRATION, never as an edit to this file, and it is only safe while the relation is still empty and no consumer has written to it. The operator should say plainly in the release ticket that rolling back returns `GET /api/integrations/bandsintown/status` and `POST /api/integrations/bandsintown/disconnect` to a 500 on an authenticated request, which is the state every deployed environment is in today - a truthful regression to a known-broken state, not a new one. Because `created_by` cascades from `auth.users`, dropping the table is also the only way to remove its rows, so the DROP must not be issued against a populated relation. `ALTER TABLE ... NO FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` and `REVOKE ... FROM anon` are NOT part of any rollback: both narrow the table's protection and the file's whole security argument is that RLS is the boundary here.
recovery.forwardFix: Any correction is a new additive migration with a higher version. Two shapes are already anticipated by this file's post-condition, so a bad forward fix cannot be applied silently: an extra policy or an unexpected grant is reported as UNEXPECTED state, and a changed column contract, constraint, index or missing grant is reported as a MISSING contract entry - both name the defect and abort the apply. Note the ordering constraint this creates: a forward fix that widens `authenticated` to INSERT/UPDATE will be reported as UNEXPECTED state by THIS file if the two are applied in the same version, so the grant change and this file's expectations must move together, which is the intended behaviour and not an obstacle. A forward fix cannot silently widen the owner-row predicates either: the rendered predicate is compared, not merely the policy's existence.
